display.name: Request Rate by Status (429s show as 4xx)
display.description: Every HTTP response the gateway returned, by status class, counted by praxis core on 100% of requests and unaffected by trace sampling. Budget denials appear as `4xx` (they are 429s), so this is the independent confirmation that a rate-limit decision actually reached the client. `5xx` here points at the upstream model or the gateway itself, not at the limiter. Source: `rate(praxis_http_requests_total[1m])` by `status_class`.

display.name: Admitted vs Denied, per Tier
display.description: Admission decisions per second, broken out by budget rule **and** decision, so you can see one tier throttling while another absorbs the same load. `admitted` was forwarded to the model; `denied` was rejected at admission with a 429 and never consumed GPU time. A 5-minute window is used deliberately: at 1 minute the denied series empties about a minute after a burst, so the result of a demo run would disappear before you looked at it. Source: `rate(praxis_ai_token_rate_limit_requests_total[5m])` by `rule` and `decision`.

display.name: Denial Rate per Tier
display.description: Fraction of each tier's requests rejected for budget over the last 5 minutes — a rate, so it decays back to zero once traffic stops. This is the panel that shows the tiers behaving differently: the free tier goes non-zero under sustained load while premium stays at 0%. Note the Token Budget dashboard's stat of the same name is a **lifetime** ratio and will keep reporting a value long after this one returns to zero; they disagree by design. Source: denied rate over total rate, per `rule`, with `clamp_min` so an idle tier reads 0% instead of dividing by zero.

display.name: Token Consumption Rate (tokens/sec)
display.description: Real tokens per second per tier, reconciled against what the model reported — not the reserved estimate. Compare against the tier's configured `capacity`: 5,000 tokens/min is ~83 tokens/sec sustainable on the free tier. It lags admission by roughly one request duration, because a reservation only settles once the response body has been parsed. Source: `rate(praxis_ai_token_rate_limit_tokens_total{kind="actual"}[1m])` by `rule`.

display.name: Estimation Accuracy: estimated vs actual vs refunded vs overage
display.description: How good the reservation estimate is. `estimated` is `reserved_tokens` charged up front at admission; `actual` is what the model reported; the difference settles as `refunded` (over-reserved, given back) or `overage` (under-reserved, charged extra). `estimated ≈ actual + refunded` by construction. A large refunded share means `reserved_tokens` sits well above real usage, which throttles bursts harder than the nominal budget implies — concurrency is bounded by the estimate even though throughput follows real usage. **If `actual` exactly equals `estimated` and refunded stays flat at zero, reconciliation is not running** — almost always because `token_rate_limit` was declared *after* `token_count` (response hooks run in reverse declared order). Source: `rate(praxis_ai_token_rate_limit_tokens_total[1m])` by `kind`.

display.name: P99 Latency by Filter Span (sampled)
display.description: Per-filter P99 latency derived from trace spans. Praxis emits one span per filter per phase, so `span_name` (`filter:<name>:<phase>`) is the breakdown key — this answers "which filter costs what", which a trace waterfall can only show one request at a time. **SAMPLED plane.** Random sampling is unbiased for percentiles, so these values are trustworthy even at a low sampling rate; the *volume* behind them is not — never read a count or rate off a span-derived panel. Empty for a scrape interval or two after first traffic is expected. Source: `histogram_quantile(0.99, traces_spanmetrics_latency_bucket)` from Tempo's metrics-generator.

display.name: Weighted Filter Cost — P99 x that filter's own call rate
display.description: Time attributable to each filter per second: its P99 multiplied by ITS OWN invocation rate, which genuinely reorders the ranking against raw P99 — a slow filter that runs rarely can matter less than a fast one on every request. **Both series come from the sampled span-metrics plane**, so under sampling the product under-reports by the sampling factor; the demo runs `sampling_rate: 1.0`, where it is exact. An earlier version multiplied every filter by `scalar(sum(rate(praxis_http_requests_total)))` — one constant for all of them, which cannot reorder anything and so could not do what this panel claims. Use it for relative ranking, not as an absolute latency budget.

spec.query: topk(10, histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (span_name, le) (rate(traces_spanmetrics_latency_bucket{service="praxis"}[5m]))) * on (span_name) group_left() sum by (span_name) (rate(traces_spanmetrics_calls_total{service="praxis"}[5m])))

display.name: Sampling Ratio Cross-Check (span plane / Prometheus plane)
display.description: Divides the span-derived request rate by the true Prometheus request rate, so it should sit at roughly the configured `sampling_rate` — ~1.0 in this demo, which sets 1.0 explicitly so the span panels have every request to work with. A reading materially **below** the configured rate means spans are being *lost* rather than sampled. The second series, span export failures to Tempo, is plotted alongside so you can tell the two apart at a glance: a drop with failures rising is a broken pipeline; a drop with failures flat is a sampler change. Both series are rates over 5 minutes and need sustained traffic to be meaningful.
